say: Today we are Model Makers. Word problems can look scary, but if we draw the story as bars, the answer often jumps out at us. A good model is like a map of the problem.
I will read a sentence. Show me the two bars with your hands. Which hand is higher? Then draw it on your whiteboard.
How did you show "3 times as many"? How did you show "altogether"?
Twenty cubes make two towers. One tower has 4 more cubes than the other. Guess: how many cubes are in each tower? Write your guess, then build it to test.
stuck: Stuck: build two towers the same height first. Then move cubes until one is 4 taller.
Confused: "Take the extra 4 cubes away first. Share what is left fairly. Then put the 4 back."
Ready for more: the Go further what-if on the slide (3 towers, 30 cubes). Or: 30 cubes where one tower is 4 times as tall as the other.

say: "A hall has 1500 seats: 645 red, 480 blue and the rest green. It is one whole cut into parts, so I draw ONE bar for 1500 and cut it into 645, 480 and a question mark. Whole take away the parts: 1500 − 645 = 855, 855 − 480 = 375. Check: 645 + 480 + 375 = 1500."
"Siti has 167 MORE than Ravi, so her bar is longer: Ravi’s bar and an extra piece of 167. Ben has 95 FEWER than Siti, so I compare Ben with Siti, not with Ravi."
"Before and after: when both girls get the same amount, both bars grow by the same piece, so the difference stays the same. I look for what stays the same."

do: Ask: "Is this a whole cut into parts, or two amounts being compared?"
Ask: "Who has more? Whose bar is longer? Longer by how much?"
Ask: "What stays the same in this story: the total or the difference?"
stuck: Hint 1: "Draw a bar for each person. Label what you know."
Hint 2: "Put a question mark on the part you need to find."
Hint 3: "Look for equal units. How many units are there altogether?"

say: "Mei and Siti are each given $5. Why does the difference between them stay the same?"
"Ravi says Mei must give Siti 38 stickers, because 85 − 47 = 38. What mistake did Ravi make?"
"Could you make 3 times as tall with 22 cubes? Why not?"
"How can a model help you check your answer?"
ask: "Mei and Siti are each given $5. Why does the difference between them stay the same?"

Both bars grow by the same piece, so the gap between their ends does not change. To check, put your answers back into the model: the parts must make the whole and the difference must match the story. Ravi gave the whole difference (38), so they would just swap places: she gives half, 19. 22 cubes cannot make 3 times as tall: we need 4 equal parts and 22 cannot be shared into 4 equal parts.

say: "You turned words into pictures today. Next time a word problem looks hard, draw it first."

p3l4-title.note: Objective: Draw bar models for part-whole, comparison, times-as-many and before-and-after word problems, and use them to solve two-step problems and check the answers. Heuristics taught: draw a model; before and after (look for what stays the same). Materials: Multilink cubes (about 30 per pair), strips of squared paper, scissors, mini whiteboards and markers. Online: Tutor builds the bars on the slides. Each child uses Lego bricks, coins or paper strips at home, and a whiteboard or paper to draw bars. Print the workbook before the lesson. Pairs work in pre-assigned breakout rooms (auto-move in, auto-close with a timer) for about 9.5 minutes of page-1 work, then return for the 60-second self-check slide. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 5 to 8 (two rounds) and three quick questions 8 to 11, explore 11 to 25 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 25 to 34.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 34.5 to 39.5, worksheet 39.5 to 71.5 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 68.5 everyone chooses), talk time 71.5 to 79 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 79 to 85, look back 85 to 88, stamp and close 88 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it. SPINE: Today's tool is Draw it. Draw a picture, bar model or number line that shows what is known and what is asked. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p3l4-tool.note: SPINE: Show for about 20 seconds, inside the opening. Today's tool is Draw it. Draw a picture, bar model or number line that shows what is known and what is asked. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p3l4-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "say it" ONCE for both: children say both answers together on three (about 30 seconds); nothing is held up to the camera. SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and say them together on three (once for both puzzles); nothing is held up to the camera. No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): 20. Listen for: The difference is 40. Ali gives half of it: 20. Then both have 50. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): $2. Listen for: Take away the extra $5: 9 − 5 = 4. Two equal bars share 4, so the pen is $2 (the book is $7). Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l4-warm1.note: Minutes 5 to 8. Arm bars. Play TWO rounds of two sentences (1 and 2, then 3 and 4). Read each sentence aloud. Children hold their two hands apart, one above the other, to show the two bars (online: in view of the camera), then draw the bars on whiteboards in 10 seconds. Click to show a model after each one (clicks reveal 1, 2, 3, 4 in order). Ask: "Whose bar is longer? How do you show the 5?" For 2: "How many equal parts does Mei have?" (3). For 3: "Altogether means we show the total with a bracket." For 4: "Fewer: Siti's bar is shorter. The dashed piece shows what she does not have." Watch for: children who draw "4 fewer" as a longer bar, and children who draw 3 times as many with 4 parts.

p3l4-warm2.note: Minutes 8 to 11. Whiteboards, show together, click to reveal. Ask "How did you do it in your head?" For 2, praise counting on (365 → 400 → 1000 is 35 + 600). For 3: "If 3 equal units make 27, one unit is 27 ÷ 3." Answers: 400, 635, 9. Three quick questions only; the other two (Ben has 40, Ali has 15 more: 55; Mei has 60, Siti has 12 fewer: 48) are on the take-home box of the Go further page in the workbook.

p3l4-explore1.note: Minutes 11 to 20. Pairs work with Multilink cubes (about 30 per pair). Online: Lego bricks, coins in two piles, or paper strips. Pairs make only the "4 more" towers (about 6.5 minutes of pair work). Let them try and adjust (move a cube from one tower to the other). Do not show the take-away-the-extra method yet: listen for pairs who find it. The "3 times as tall" towers are the first debrief question, done together on the shared screen. Ready for more: the Go further card, or 30 cubes where one tower is 4 times as tall (6 and 24). GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): Make 3 towers from 30 cubes, each 2 cubes taller than the last. How tall is each? (Then 3 taller.) Answer: 30 cubes: 8, 10, 12 (3 towers, take away 2 + 4 = 6, share 24 into 3). With 3 taller each time: 7, 10, 13 (30 - 9 = 21, 21 / 3 = 7). Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l4-explore2.note: Minutes 20 to 25. Gather the pairs. Take ideas, then show with cubes. Answers: 1) (Done together on the shared screen with cubes or a drawing.) 5 and 15: together the towers make 4 equal parts of 5 (1 part and 3 parts). 2) Take away the extra 4 (16 left), share 16 into two equal towers of 8, then put the 4 back: 8 and 12. Check 8 + 12 = 20 and 12 − 8 = 4. The question "Could you make 3 times as tall with 22 cubes?" (no: we need 4 equal parts, and 22 cannot be shared into 4 equal parts) has moved to talk time. Then say: "Cubes are great, but big numbers need too many cubes. Today we draw the towers as bars: bar models."

p3l4-we1.note: Teach the first heuristic: DRAW A MODEL. Click 1 builds the bar, then the steps. Ask before the bar appears: "Is this one thing cut into parts, or two things being compared?" (one whole: the hall). Think-aloud: "It is one whole cut into parts, so I draw ONE bar for 1500 and cut it into 645, 480 and a question mark. Whole take away the parts: 1500 − 645 = 855, 855 − 480 = 375. Check: 645 + 480 + 375 = 1500." Point out that the ? part looks a bit smaller than 480 on the model: a quick sense check.

p3l4-try1.note: Whiteboards: draw the bar, then the answer. a) 900 − 275 = 625 cm. b) 1200 − 450 − 380 = 370. c) Here the parts are known and the whole is the ?: 368 + 245 = 613. Ask: "Where does the ? go this time?"

p3l4-we2.note: Click to build each bar. Before each click ask: "Is this bar longer or shorter? Than whose bar? By how much?" Think-aloud: "Siti has 167 MORE than Ravi, so her bar is Ravi's bar and an extra piece of 167: 236 + 167 = 403. Ben has 95 FEWER than Siti, so I compare Ben with Siti, not with Ravi. His bar is Siti's bar with 95 missing: 403 − 95 = 308." Common mistake: 236 − 95 (comparing with the wrong person). Point at the words "than Siti".

p3l4-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) 125 + 60 = 185. b) Ravi 342 − 87 = 255, altogether 342 + 255 = 597 (two steps). c) A trick question: the model shows the difference is already given, 135 g. Nobody needs to work out Box B. Praise children who spotted it from their model.

p3l4-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Comparing with the wrong person (Ben has 79 fewer than ALI, not Mei), or drawing "more than" as a shorter bar. (2) Times as many: dividing the total by 3 instead of by 3 + 1 = 4 units. (3) Make them equal: giving the whole difference instead of half of it.

p3l4-break.note: Five minutes. Mix the calls quickly. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p3l4-teachunits.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3 is times as many). "4 times as many" means Ben's bar is 4 of Ali's bars. Ask before step 1: "How many units altogether?" Many children say 4. Point to the model and count: Ali's 1 and Ben's 4 make 5. Then share 175 into 5 equal units (175 ÷ 5 = 35).

p3l4-ws1.note: Minutes 41.5 to 54.5. Pairs work together. Walk around and ask "Is it a whole cut into parts, or a comparison?" For Q2, check pairs subtract 79 from ALI's number. For Q3, check they use 4 units. PAGE 1 CLOCK (41.5 to 54.5): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 9.5 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l4-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: 1250 − 486 − 378 = 386; 486 − 378 = 108. Q2: Ali 345 + 128 = 473; Ben 473 − 79 = 394; total 345 + 473 + 394 = 1212. Q3: 248 ÷ 4 = 62; Siti 3 × 62 = 186; the difference is 2 units = 124. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l4-teachtd.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). This is the explore idea with bigger numbers: take away the extra, share equally, give the extra back. Cover Mei's yellow piece with your hand: "Now the bars are the same. What do they add up to?" (74). Ask: "Why not 90 ÷ 2 = 45 each?" (Then Mei would not have 16 more.)

p3l4-teachgive.note: Teach before worksheet Q5. Act it out first with cubes: 6 and 2. "How many must I move to make them equal?" Many say 4 (the difference). Try it: 6 − 4 = 2 and 2 + 4 = 6, they just swapped! Move 2 instead: 4 and 4. So give HALF the difference. Then click to build the model. What stays the same: the total.

p3l4-ws2.note: Children work alone and draw their own models in the dashed boxes: Q4 and Q5(a) are the page-2 work (about 7.5 minutes). Q5(b) (Ravi's mistake) and Q6 are marked (if time): Ravi's mistake is discussed in talk time. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson.

p3l4-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains with their model. Q4 check: 63 + 87 = 150 and 87 − 63 = 24. Q5: difference 85 − 47 = 38, give half: 19. Ravi's 38 leaves Mei with 47 and Siti with 85. Q6: after Grandma, Ali has $55 and Ben $28, so $55 − $28 = $27; before, $45 − $18 = $27. Both boys got the same amount, so the difference stays the same. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l4-stretch.note: For children who choose Think harder. Answers: 1) Flour 3 kg, rice 6 kg (9 − 3 = 6, 6 ÷ 2 = 3). 2) 60: the difference is 2 units and Ben gave half of it, so 1 unit = 20; Ravi had 20, Ben 60 (then 40 and 40). 3) 300 g: take away the two extras, 1700 − 800 = 900 for 3 equal units, 900 ÷ 3 = 300 (flour 700 g each).

p3l4-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 10. At first Ben 1 unit, Ali 3 units; 4 units = 120, so Ben 30 and Ali 90. The total is still 120, but now Ali has 2 parts and Ben 1 part, so 3 equal parts = 120 and each part is 40: Ben 40 and Ali 80. Ben went from 30 to 40, so Ali gave 10. 2) Pen $5, box $10. The second bill is $10 more because it has 2 more pens, so 2 pens cost $10 and 1 pen costs $5. Then 3 pens cost $15 and the box costs $10.

p3l4-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What stays the same? What do we know? For Q1: how many equal parts are there AFTER? For Q2: what is different about the two bills? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p3l4-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1 is a before-and-after problem where the RATIO changes: the total stays the same (120), so find the new unit first (3 equal parts), then compare Ben before and after. Q2: when two bills differ in only one thing, the difference in price tells you the price of that one thing.

p3l4-teachsame.note: Talk time (moved here from the worksheet): this slide is the whole-class discussion "what stays the same?", the second heuristic, BEFORE AND AFTER. Workbook Q6 (Grandma gives both boys $10) is now an (if time) question that builds on it. Ask: "When both girls get $5, what happens to the gap between them?" Show with two cube towers, add 2 cubes to each: the gap does not change. Then click the model. Check aloud: Siti $12 + $5 = $17, Mei $30 + $5 = $35, and $35 − $17 = $18, the same gap as before. Compare with Q5: when one gives to the other, the TOTAL stays the same; when both get the same, the DIFFERENCE stays the same.

p3l4-talk.note: Minutes 73 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. This talk time also holds the slide before it (what stays the same?). Expected: both bars grow by the same piece, so the gap between their ends does not change. Extra questions moved here: (1) Ravi's mistake, workbook Q5(b): "Ravi says Mei must give Siti 38, because 85 − 47 = 38. What mistake did he make?" (38 is the whole difference: they would just swap; she gives half, 19). (2) "Could you make 3 times as tall with 22 cubes? Why not?" (4 equal parts: 22 cannot be shared into 4 equal parts). Follow-up: "When Mei GIVES Siti $5, what stays the same?" (the total). "How can a model help you check your answer?" (put the answers back: the parts must make the whole and the difference must match). TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l4-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: 60. 4 units = 80, so 1 unit = 20, and Ali has 3 units. Watch for 80 ÷ 3. Extension: write your own before-and-after story, draw its model and check it, then swap with a partner. Answers stay on the child’s own paper and are ticked against the answer slide. Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l4-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 85 to 88. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
